ABSTRACT 
The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), developed by the National Payments Corporation of 
India (NPCI), has revolutionized retail digital payments, facilitating over 14 billion instant 
bank-to-bank settlements monthly. Despite this exponential adoption, UPI’s real-time 
settlement architecture introduces severe systemic vulnerabilities. Unlike traditional credit 
card payment systems that incorporate multi-hour clearing windows, multi-day dispute 
cycles, or chargeback mechanisms, UPI transactions settle with immediate finality between 
underlying savings accounts. Cyber-criminals exploit this irreversible settlement through 
sophisticated attack vectors including social engineering phishing, SIM-swapping, remote 
screen-sharing takeovers, off-hours velocity drains, and high-velocity money laundering 
routed through complex multi-hop mule account rings. Conventional banking defenses rely 
predominantly on static, rigid rule engines (e.g., rigid threshold filters) or post-facto batch 
audits (T+1 clearing analysis). These approaches induce unacceptably high False Positive 
Rates (FPR), causing severe user friction for legitimate transactions while consistently failing 
to intercept rapid, micro-amount fraudulent attacks before financial finality occurs. 
To resolve these foundational security and usability bottlenecks, this project presents “UPI 
PayGuard AI”, an enterprise-grade, pre-transaction fraud detection, prevention, and 
biometric verification platform engineered to evaluate contextual risk in sub-50 ms prior to 
payment settlement. UPI PayGuard AI establishes a unified defense pipeline integrating five 
synchronized security paradigms: (1) Continuous Behavioral Scoring: Quantifying 
multidimensional deviation from personalized spending averages across amount ratios, 
rolling velocity bursts, and historical transaction frequency; (2) Graph-Theoretic 
Counterparty Audits: Constructing relational financial transaction graphs using Cytoscape.js 
and NetworkX to evaluate node in-degree/out-degree centrality, high fan-in clusters, and 
circular layering loops characteristic of mule networks; (3) Multi-Tier Adaptive Step-Up 
Security: Dynamically graduating authentication demands across calibrated risk tiers—Auto-
Approve (0–30%), SMS/WhatsApp Cryptographic OTP Step-Up (31–60%), Deep Facial 
Biometric Attestation (61–85%), and Instant Security Freeze (86–100%); (4) Deep Facial 
Biometrics: Employing lightweight OpenCV YuNet neural detection and SFace feature 
extraction to map facial landmarks into normalized 128-dimensional unit vectors evaluated 
via Cosine Similarity against enrolled templates; and (5) Grounded Explainable AI (XAI): 
Presenting deterministic, mathematically auditable ledger proof records directly from the

underlying relational store to explain every risk assessment to end-users and compliance 
officers. 
The system architecture is implemented using a high-performance three-tier service-oriented 
stack: a reactive client application built with React 18 and Vite styled with modern CSS 
design systems; an asynchronous application server running Express.js on Node.js; an 
embedded, zero-latency transactional database engine running SQLite (`fraud_detection.db`) 
with strict dual-store schema separation between user biometric credentials and transaction 
audit trails; and a Python-powered machine learning inference engine evaluating optimized 
gradient-boosted decision trees. Extensive empirical benchmarking across candidate 
algorithms—Hist Gradient Boosting, Extra Trees, Random Forest, XGBoost, and Logistic 
Regression—reveals that gradient-boosted ensemble architectures achieve state-of-the-art 
predictive performance on imbalanced UPI transaction streams, recording 97.4% to 100% 
Precision, 98.6% to 100% Recall, 0.993 to 1.0 F1-Score, and a 1.0 ROC-AUC score under 
cost-sensitive scale position weighting (`scale_pos_weight = N_neg / N_pos`). The end-to-
end evaluation latency averages 35.0 ms, guaranteeing sub-second transaction authorization. 
Furthermore, UPI PayGuard AI directly advances United Nations Sustainable Development 
Goals: SDG 8 (Decent Work & Economic Growth) by safeguarding digital financial stability, 
SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation & Infrastructure) through resilient cloud-native security, and 
SDG 16 (Peace, Justice & Strong Institutions) by eradicating illicit financial flows.

Chapter 1 
INTRODUCTION 
1.1 MOTIVATION 
In the contemporary global financial landscape, digital retail payment systems have 
undergone a profound paradigm shift from conventional branch-centric banking and delayed 
credit clearing toward instantaneous, peer-to-peer (P2P) and merchant electronic payment 
networks. At the forefront of this global financial technology revolution stands the Unified 
Payments Interface (UPI), architected and governed by the National Payments Corporation of 
India (NPCI). Operating atop immediate payment infrastructure, UPI allows users to 
seamlessly link multiple bank accounts to a single mobile smartphone application, facilitating 
instantaneous, 24x7x365 fund transfers using virtual payment addresses (UPI IDs), mobile 
numbers, or dynamic Quick Response (QR) codes. Monthly transaction telemetry released by 
NPCI indicates that UPI routinely processes over 14 billion individual transactions, 
accounting for over 75% of all retail electronic payment volumes across the Republic of 
India and settling hundreds of billions of dollars in gross monetary value annually. 
However, the foundational architectural attributes that have propelled UPI’s unprecedented 
ubiquity—namely, sub-second settlement speed, zero-cost consumer fees, and irrevocable 
direct bank-to-bank debiting—have also precipitated severe, unprecedented cyber-security 
vulnerabilities. In classical credit card or card-not-present payment schemes, a multi-hour or 
multi-day settlement window exists alongside robust legal chargeback mechanisms. When an 
unauthorized card transaction occurs, financial institutions can freeze settlements, place holds 
on acquiring merchant accounts, and initiate forensic dispute resolutions before irreversible 
cash outflow happens. In stark contrast, UPI transfers settle with instantaneous finality 
directly between the savings accounts of the payer and the payee. Once a sender confirms a 
transfer using their 4-digit or 6-digit static UPI PIN, the funds are irrevocably debited and 
instantly credited to the counterparty account. 
Cyber-syndicates and financial fraudsters have aggressively weaponized this instantaneous 
finality. Organized financial crime networks deploy high-velocity layering schemes wherein 
defrauded capital is routed through automated chains of compromised 'mule accounts' within 
tens of seconds, effectively obfuscating the audit trail and cash-out points before victims or 
banking anti-money laundering (AML) analysts can intervene. Furthermore, the human 
attack surface has expanded massively through sophisticated social engineering:

impersonation of utility providers, phishing calls demanding remote screen-sharing tool 
installations (e.g., AnyDesk, TeamViewer), fraudulent merchant QR overlays, and off-hours 
account takeover bursts executed while account holders sleep. Consequently, real-time pre-
transaction fraud prevention has transformed from an optional banking enhancement into a 
critical national security imperative. 
1.2 PROBLEM STATEMENT 
Existing commercial fraud detection platforms and core banking solutions deployed across 
digital payment networks suffer from critical architectural, algorithmic, and operational 
bottlenecks that render them incapable of intercepting modern UPI fraud vectors. 
Specifically, the core challenges addressed in this research and engineering endeavor 
encompass: 
 
Severe Inefficacy of Static Rule-Based Engines: Mainstream banking security 
frameworks rely heavily on rigid threshold-based rules (e.g., IF transfer_amount > 
₹50,000 THEN flag). Fraudsters easily bypass these by structuring illicit fund extractions 
into multiple micro-transactions (e.g., ₹9,500 transfers) beneath threshold radars. 
Conversely, static rules trigger massive False Positive Rates (FPR) when legitimate users 
make large seasonal purchases, causing user attrition and severe alert fatigue. 
 
Post-Facto Forensic Auditing Latency: Most advanced anomaly detection models in 
existing banking backends execute asynchronously in post-settlement batch workflows 
(T+1 clearing audits or hourly batch runs). While effective for regulatory reporting, post-
facto detection is completely powerless to prevent irreversible monetary theft on instant 
settlement rails. 
 
Failure to Exploit Relational Network Topology: Traditional fraud scoring models 
evaluate transactions in total isolation as independent feature vectors, completely 
ignoring graph topology. They cannot perceive multi-hop money mule chains, circular 
layering cycles, or sudden spikes in payee in-degree centrality (high fan-in clusters from 
dozens of unrelated senders). 
 
Vulnerability of Static Credential Authentication: The standard 4-digit or 6-digit UPI 
PIN is vulnerable to shoulder surfing, malware keylogging, remote screen scraping, and 
coercive phishing. Once the PIN is compromised, standard applications offer zero 
secondary defense. 
 
The Explainability Black-Box Dilemma in Banking: While deep learning algorithms 
can output fraud probabilities, their internal mechanics remain impenetrable black boxes. 
Financial regulations (RBI circulars, ISO 27001) mandate that automated interventions 
denying customer fund access must provide grounded, auditable evidence.

1.3 SCOPE OF THE PROJECT 
The scope of this project encompasses the design, formal mathematical modeling, full-stack 
implementation, empirical validation, and viva defense of “UPI PayGuard AI”, an intelligent, 
pre-transaction fraud prevention platform. The specific functional and technical boundaries 
of the system include: 
 
Sub-50ms Pre-Transaction Machine Learning Evaluation: Engineering high-speed 
feature extraction pipelines coupled with optimized gradient-boosted decision tree 
ensembles (Hist Gradient Boosting, Extra Trees, XGBoost) to classify transaction risk 
before payment settlement. 
 
Continuous Behavioral & Habitual Profiling: Tracking sender-specific historical 
spending distributions, 24-hour diurnal activity histograms, and rapid velocity burst 
counters to detect abnormal behavioral deviations. 
 
Relational Counterparty & Graph Centrality Auditing: Integrating graph algorithms 
to verify counterparty establishment, identify first-time recipients, and compute fan-in 
centrality to detect mule accounts in real time. 
 
Multi-Tier Adaptive Step-Up Security Framework: Dynamically enforcing graduated 
verification challenges based on four calibrated risk tiers: Auto-Approve (0–30%), 
Cryptographic SMS OTP (31–60%), Live Deep Facial Biometric Attestation (61–85%), 
and Instant Security Freeze (86–100%). 
 
Deep Facial Biometric Verification Pipeline: Embedding OpenCV YuNet neural face 
detection and SFace feature extraction to extract normalized 128-dimensional unit vectors 
and execute Cosine Similarity matching against enrolled reference vectors. 
 
Grounded Explainable AI (XAI) & Audit Ledger: Formulating deterministic rule 
engines that query underlying relational tables to render auditable historical evidence tiles 
justifying every risk assessment. 
1.4 RELATION TO PREVIOUS WORK AND PRESENT 
DEVELOPMENTS 
Early financial anomaly detection literature focused primarily on rule-based expert systems 
and statistical outliers in credit card datasets (Carminati et al., 2015 [1]; Dal Pozzolo et al., 
2018 [2]). While these studies established statistical baselines, their assumptions relied 
heavily on credit card clearance delays and chargeback safety nets that do not apply to real-
time UPI networks. Subsequent advancements introduced supervised machine learning 
algorithms, notably Random Forests and Support Vector Machines (SVMs), for payment 
fraud detection (Bhattacharyya et al., 2011 [3]). However, standard classifiers struggled with

severe class imbalance (where fraud represents < 1% of transactions) and exhibited inference 
latencies exceeding hundreds of milliseconds. 
In recent years, the emergence of graph-theoretic modeling and Graph Neural Networks 
(GNNs) demonstrated the critical importance of relational connectivity in financial fraud 
investigations (Weber et al., 2019 [4]; Wang et al., 2021 [5]). Nevertheless, existing graph 
approaches remain predominantly offline batch systems running over graph databases like 
Neo4j, which are incapable of sub-50ms query execution during live payment authorizations. 
Simultaneously, deep facial biometrics have achieved state-of-the-art verification precision 
through architectures such as FaceNet (Schroff et al., 2015 [6]) and SFace (Sheng et al., 2021 
[7]), yet such biometric systems have operated exclusively as standalone onboarding tools 
rather than dynamic, in-transaction step-up challenges. 
UPI PayGuard AI advances the current state of the art by harmoniously synthesizing these 
disparate engineering disciplines into a unified, ultra-low-latency service-oriented 
architecture. By combining tree-based gradient boosting models, in-memory graph centrality 
lookups, 128-dimensional deep facial vector cosine similarity matching, and grounded XAI 
auditability, UPI PayGuard AI bridges the critical void between instant transaction 
convenience and adaptive payment defense.

statuses). This design prevents credential leakage even in the event of targeted analytical 
ledger audits.

-- SQLite Relational Schema for fraud_detection.db 
 
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users ( 
    user_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, 
    full_name TEXT NOT NULL, 
    email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL, 
    phone_number TEXT NOT NULL, 
    password_hash TEXT NOT NULL, 
    salt TEXT NOT NULL, 
    account_id TEXT NOT NULL, 
    face_embedding TEXT, -- JSON-serialized 128-D unit vector 
    template_hash TEXT, 
    created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP 
); 
 
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS accounts ( 
    account_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, 
    account_name TEXT NOT NULL, 
    upi_id TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL, 
    bank_name TEXT NOT NULL, 
    account_type TEXT NOT NULL, 
    current_balance REAL DEFAULT 0.0, 
    trust_score REAL DEFAULT 80.0, 
    account_status TEXT DEFAULT 'ACTIVE', 
    created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP 
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS account_behavior ( 
    account_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, 
    total_transactions INTEGER DEFAULT 0, 
    average_transaction_amount REAL DEFAULT 0.0, 
    maximum_transaction_amount REAL DEFAULT 0.0, 
    night_transactions INTEGER DEFAULT 0, 
    frequent_receiver_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0, 
    FOREIGN KEY(account_id) REFERENCES accounts(account_id) 
); 
 
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS transactions ( 
    transaction_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, 
    sender_account TEXT NOT NULL, 
    receiver_account TEXT NOT NULL, 
    amount REAL NOT NULL, 
    payment_mode TEXT DEFAULT 'UPI_P2P', 
    timestamp DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, 
    status TEXT DEFAULT 'PENDING', 
    fraud_probability REAL DEFAULT 0.0, 
    risk_level TEXT DEFAULT 'LOW', 
    is_fraud INTEGER DEFAULT 0, 
    FOREIGN KEY(sender_account) REFERENCES accounts(account_id), 
    FOREIGN KEY(receiver_account) REFERENCES accounts(account_id) 
); 
 
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_txn_sender ON transactions(sender_account); 
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_txn_timestamp ON transactions(timestamp); 
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_txn_fraud ON transactions(is_fraud);
